title: Manage by stages
blurb: Explain why a PRINCE2 project is planned, monitored and controlled one stage at a time, how many stages it needs and what drives stage length.
question: A project board wants to approve a two-year project in one go and skip any further reviews. Which principle would that break, and why?

teach.body: Formally: a PRINCE2 project is planned, monitored and controlled on a stage-by-stage basis. In plain English: the board does not hand over the whole project in one go. It commits to one management stage, reviews the results, and then decides whether to commit to the next. Each stage end is a review and decision point.

teach.h: A project of three management stages
teach.caption: At least two stages: initiation first, then one or more delivery stages. Closing happens inside the final stage; it is not a stage of its own.

items: Review and decision points let the board assess viability at set intervals instead of letting the project run uncontrolled.
The project is properly initiated before any delivery work starts.
Authority is delegated to the project manager one stage at a time; within tolerance, the PM adapts as needed.
Only the near future can be planned in detail, so a high-level project plan is paired with a detailed stage plan.

teach.caption: Number and length of stages depend on the planning horizon, decision points needed, risk and complexity. Stage ends can line up with outside events such as the budget cycle.

teach.h: Two levels of plan for two horizons
head: Plan
Covers
Detail
rows: Detailed, made near the end of the previous stage
Detailed, made in starting up a project

teach.h: What happens at each stage boundary
teach.caption: Stage boundaries are also good points to review how people work together and adapt the team.

teach.body: Northgate Bus Company is rebuilding a depot. Project manager Chloe Brennan proposes three stages: initiation, demolition and groundworks, then construction and handover. Because groundworks carry the most uncertainty, she keeps that stage short, ending it in March to line up with the company's budget round. At that boundary, executive Martin Shaw's board reviews the end stage report and the updated business case before authorizing construction.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) Manage by stages is about planning and decision points stage by stage; SETTING TOLERANCES is manage by exception. (2) Closing a project happens inside the final stage; it is not a separate stage, and managing a stage boundary is not used at the end of the final stage. (3) The minimum is two stages, not three.

items: Planned, monitored and controlled stage by stage, with board decision points at each stage end.
At least two stages: the initiation stage plus one or more delivery stages.
Shorter stages give more control; longer stages reduce the burden on senior management.
Project plan for the whole project; detailed stage plan for the current stage (planning horizon).
Authority is delegated to the project manager one stage at a time.

summary: You can now explain how manage by stages gives the board decision points, why there are at least two stages, and how planning horizon, risk and complexity shape stage length. You can also separate it from manage by exception.

A.q: What is the minimum number of management stages in a PRINCE2 project?
options: Four
Three
Two
One
A.why: There must be at least two stages: the initiation stage and one or more delivery stages.

whyNot.0: Four is a design choice, not a minimum.
whyNot.1: Three is common, but the minimum is two.
whyNot.3: A single stage would mean no initiation stage before delivery.

A.q: Which statement describes the manage by stages principle?
options: Tolerances are set for each level of plan
Products are defined before work starts
The project is planned and controlled stage by stage
Delivery is split into fixed-length iterations
A.why: A PRINCE2 project is planned, monitored and controlled on a stage-by-stage basis (manual 2.4).

whyNot.0: Setting tolerances is manage by exception.
whyNot.1: Defining products before work is focus on products.
whyNot.3: Iterations are a delivery technique; management stages are board decision points and need not be fixed length.

A.q: What is the first stage of every PRINCE2 project?
options: The pre-project stage
The first delivery stage
The starting up stage
The initiation stage
A.why: The first management stage is always the initiation stage, so the project is properly initiated before delivery starts.

whyNot.0: Pre-project work (starting up a project) happens before the project's stages begin.
whyNot.2: Starting up a project is a pre-project process, not a stage.

B.q:
Which two statements about stage length are correct?
1. Shorter stages give the board more control.
2. Longer stages reduce the burden on senior management.
3. Every stage must last the same length of time.
4. Stage length is fixed by the business layer.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Shorter stages give more control (1); longer stages reduce the burden on senior management (2). Length is chosen to suit size, complexity and risk.

whyNot.1: Statement 3 is false: stages can differ in length.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: stages are planned within the project, not fixed by the business layer.
whyNot.3: Both are false: stages vary in length, and their length is a project planning decision.

B.q: Why does PRINCE2 combine a high-level project plan with a detailed stage plan?
options: Only the near future can be planned in detail
The board approves the stage plans in advance
Team managers need the project plan for their work
The project plan is replaced at each boundary
B.why: The planning horizon means only the near future can be planned in detail, so detailed stage plans sit under a high-level project plan.

whyNot.1: Each stage plan is approved near the end of the previous stage, not all in advance.
whyNot.2: Team managers work from work packages and team plans.
whyNot.3: The project plan is updated at each boundary, not replaced.

B.q: A project manager ends a stage in March so that the board's decision coincides with the organization's budget-setting cycle. What does this illustrate?
options: Using exception plans to reset the budget
Aligning stage ends with external influences
Tailoring away a stage to save management time
Setting cost tolerance for the next stage
B.why: Stage ends can be aligned with external influences such as the budget cycle, to make their impact clear to the board.

whyNot.0: Exception plans respond to forecast tolerance breaches, not budget cycles.
whyNot.2: No stage is removed; the stage end is placed to match the cycle.
whyNot.3: Setting tolerance is manage by exception and is not what timing the stage end does.

C.q: Where in the lifecycle are closing activities carried out, and is a stage boundary process run at the end?
options: In a separate closure stage; yes, a boundary is run
Inside the final stage; no boundary is run at its end
Inside the final stage; yes, a boundary is run
In a separate closure stage; no boundary is run
C.why: Closing a project is part of the final stage, not a stage of its own, and managing a stage boundary is not used at the end of the final stage.

whyNot.0: Closure is not its own stage, and no boundary process follows the final stage.
whyNot.2: Closure is inside the final stage, but no stage boundary is run at its end.
whyNot.3: Closure is not a separate stage.

C.q: How does manage by stages support manage by exception?
options: It sets the tolerance levels for each work package
It replaces exception reports with end stage reports
It delegates authority to the PM a stage at a time
It lets the PM approve the next stage plan
C.why: Manage by stages delegates authority to the project manager one stage at a time; within stage tolerance, the PM can adjust as needed.

whyNot.0: The PM sets work package tolerances; that is manage by exception, not stages.
whyNot.1: Exception reports are still needed when a stage is forecast to exceed tolerance.
whyNot.3: The board approves the next stage plan when authorizing the next stage.

C.q: In which process is the initiation stage plan prepared, and where are later stage plans prepared?
options: Starting up a project; managing a stage boundary
Initiating a project; controlling a stage
Starting up a project; initiating a project
Directing a project; managing a stage boundary
C.why: The initiation stage plan is made in starting up a project; every later stage plan is made in managing a stage boundary near the end of the previous stage.

whyNot.1: Initiation creates the project plan; controlling a stage does not prepare the next stage plan.
whyNot.2: Initiating a project produces the project plan, not later stage plans.
whyNot.3: Directing a project approves plans; the project manager prepares them.

reteach.title: A road trip booked one leg at a time
reteach.question: You are driving across a country you don't know. Would you book every hotel for three weeks before setting off?

blocks.h: Plan the next leg in detail
blocks.body: You would sketch the whole route, book tonight's hotel in detail, and decide each evening whether to carry on, change course or turn back. That is manage by stages: a high-level project plan for the whole journey, a detailed stage plan for the next leg, and a board decision at the end of each leg. The first leg is always initiation: checking the route before committing to the drive.

blocks.h: Each leg ends with a decision

items.label: Initiation stage: plan the trip properly

blocks.text: Short legs give more control but more stops; long legs mean fewer stops but less control.

explain.body: Each stage end lets the board review progress and viability and decide whether to continue, rather than let the project run uncontrolled.

test.q: What do stage boundaries give the project board?
options: Daily control of the teams' work
Points to review and decide on the project
A chance to rewrite the project mandate
Authority to set the business layer's tolerances
test.why: Stages provide review and decision points so the board can assess viability at defined intervals.

whyNot.0: Day-to-day control is the project manager's job.
whyNot.2: The mandate comes from the business layer before the project starts.
whyNot.3: Project tolerances are set by the business layer, not the board.

explain.body: The initiation stage is always first, so the project is properly initiated before delivery. Then come one or more delivery stages.

test.q: Why is the initiation stage always the first stage?
options: So the business case can be confirmed
So the board can appoint the executive
So the project is properly initiated first
So the closing activities can be planned
test.why: Manage by stages ensures the project is properly initiated before delivery work starts.

whyNot.0: Benefits are confirmed mostly after closure; initiation develops the full business case.
whyNot.1: The business layer appoints the executive, in starting up a project.
whyNot.3: Closing activities are planned in the final stage's plan.

explain.body: Shorter stages mean more control; longer stages mean less burden on senior management. The choice depends on planning horizon, risk, complexity and size.

test.q: A project carries high uncertainty in its next phase. What does manage by stages suggest?
options: A longer stage to save board time
A single stage for all delivery work
Wider tolerances for the next stage
A shorter stage to increase control
test.why: Shorter stages give the board more control, which suits risky, uncertain work.

whyNot.0: Longer stages reduce board burden but give less control.
whyNot.1: One long delivery stage reduces control further.
whyNot.2: Tolerance width is a manage by exception decision.

explain.body: Only the near future can be planned in detail. So there is a high-level project plan for the whole project and a detailed stage plan for the current stage.

test.q: Which plan gives the detailed view of the current stage?
options: Project plan
Team plan
Exception plan
Stage plan
test.why: The stage plan is the detailed plan for the current stage; the project plan stays high level.

whyNot.0: The project plan covers the whole project at a high level.
whyNot.1: A team plan is produced by a team manager to organize a team's work, not to plan the whole stage.
whyNot.2: An exception plan replaces a plan forecast to exceed tolerance.
